VideoTitle: Jon Stewart REAMS Bill Maher's 'Cancel Culture' Take | Krystal Kyle & Friends Podcast
CommentText:
Jon's part about the Internet "democratizing" criticism feels spot on to me. Think of all these comedians saying "twenty years ago, I made this joke and everyone laughed. Now I'm being cancelled!". Back in the day, they made XYZ joke to an audience that paid to see them, and that's the only people who saw it. If they were really big, they got an HBO special or something watched by people who like them. They got primarily positive feedback because their audiences were curated. And not curated by some intentional gatekeepers, but curated by the simple fact that you had to buy a ticket and go to a show or at least sit down and tune in to the specific channel to watch the comedian you wanted in lieu of something else. The audience of that comedian were the people who liked that comedian, the people who liked the types of jokes that comedian told. 

Now, their jokes just pop into our social media feeds or whatever regardless of whether we sought them out or not, and it takes two clicks to give our opinion. Suddenly, their jokes are getting feedback from ALL types of people, not just those who likes that comedian's jokes. And when your audience is suddenly not just your fans, suddenly your universal adoration is going to give way to something a bit more, well, balanced at best.

Think of Trump for example. When he goes to his rallies, what does he get? Frenzied cheers. Fairly expected since the people who attend Trump rallies are his fans. But remember when he was announced at that baseball game, which was NOT nearly 100% packed with Trump supporters? Remember how hard he got booed? That's not cancel culture, as these comedians seem to think it is. That's just having an audience that's not made up almost entirely of your fans.

import os
from tkinter import *
from tkinter import filedialog, colorchooser, font, messagebox

def center_window():
    window_width = 800
    window_height = 600
    screen_width = window.winfo_screenwidth()
    screen_height = window.winfo_screenheight()
    x = (screen_width // 2) - (window_width // 2)
    y = (screen_height // 2) - (window_height // 2)
    window.geometry(f"{window_width}x{window_height}+{x}+{y}")

def change_color():
    color = colorchooser.askcolor(title="Pick a color")[1]
    if color:
        text_area.config(fg=color)

def change_font(*args):
    text_area.config(font=(font_name.get(), size_box.get()))

def new_file():
    if check_unsaved_changes():
        window.title("Untitled")
        text_area.delete(1.0, END)

def open_file():
    if check_unsaved_changes():
        file = filedialog.askopenfilename(defaultextension=".txt",
                                          filetypes=[("All Files", "*.*"),
                                                     ("Text Documents", "*.txt")])
        if file:
            window.title(os.path.basename(file))
            text_area.delete(1.0, END)
            with open(file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file_content:
                text_area.insert(1.0, file_content.read())

def save_file():
    file = filedialog.asksaveasfilename(initialfile='untitled.txt',
                                        defaultextension=".txt",
                                        filetypes=[("All Files", "*.*"),
                                                   ("Text Documents", "*.txt")])
    if file:
        with open(file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file_content:
            file_content.write(text_area.get(1.0, END))
        window.title(os.path.basename(file))

def save_file_as():
    save_file()

def check_unsaved_changes():
    if text_area.edit_modified():
        response = messagebox.askyesnocancel("Save Changes",
                                             "Do you want to save changes to the current file?")
        if response:
            save_file()
            return True
        elif response is None:
            return False
    return True

def quit_app():
    if check_unsaved_changes():
        window.quit()

def cut():
    text_area.event_generate("<<Cut>>")

def copy():
    text_area.event_generate("<<Copy>>")

def paste():
    text_area.event_generate("<<Paste>>")

def undo():
    text_area.event_generate("<<Undo>>")

def redo():
    text_area.event_generate("<<Redo>>")

def about():
    messagebox.showinfo("About", "This is a simple text editor created using Python and Tkinter by Sai Pranav.")

def update_status_bar(event=None):
    line, column = text_area.index(INSERT).split('.')
    status_bar.config(text=f"Line: {line}, Column: {column}")

window = Tk()
window.title("Text Editor")

center_window()

font_name = StringVar(value="Arial")
font_size = StringVar(value="20")

text_area = Text(window, wrap=WORD, font=(font_name.get(), font_size.get()), undo=True)
text_area.pack(fill=BOTH, expand=True)
text_area.bind("<KeyRelease>", update_status_bar)

scroll_bar = Scrollbar(text_area)
scroll_bar.pack(side=RIGHT, fill=Y)
text_area.config(yscrollcommand=scroll_bar.set)
scroll_bar.config(command=text_area.yview)

status_bar = Label(window, text="Line: 1, Column: 1", anchor=E)
status_bar.pack(fill=X, side=BOTTOM)

menu_bar = Menu(window)
window.config(menu=menu_bar)

file_menu = Menu(menu_bar, tearoff=0)
menu_bar.add_cascade(label="File", menu=file_menu)
file_menu.add_command(label="New", command=new_file)
file_menu.add_command(label="Open", command=open_file)
file_menu.add_command(label="Save", command=save_file)
file_menu.add_command(label="Save As", command=save_file_as)
file_menu.add_separator()
file_menu.add_command(label="Exit", command=quit_app)

edit_menu = Menu(menu_bar, tearoff=0)
menu_bar.add_cascade(label="Edit", menu=edit_menu)
edit_menu.add_command(label="Undo", command=undo)
edit_menu.add_command(label="Redo", command=redo)
edit_menu.add_separator()
edit_menu.add_command(label="Cut", command=cut)
edit_menu.add_command(label="Copy", command=copy)
edit_menu.add_command(label="Paste", command=paste)

help_menu = Menu(menu_bar, tearoff=0)
menu_bar.add_cascade(label="Help", menu=help_menu)
help_menu.add_command(label="About", command=about)

frame = Frame(window)
frame.pack(fill=X)

color_button = Button(frame, text="Color", command=change_color)
color_button.pack(side=LEFT, padx=5)

font_box = OptionMenu(frame, font_name, *font.families(), command=change_font)
font_box.pack(side=LEFT, padx=5)

size_box = Spinbox(frame, from_=8, to=72, textvariable=font_size, command=change_font)
size_box.pack(side=LEFT, padx=5)

window.protocol("WM_DELETE_WINDOW", quit_app)
window.mainloop()

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge #74: Clock with p5.js
CommentText:
I like the end result, but I would modify some things about the code:
- I don't think it's such a good idea to redraw the clock on each frame. Perhaps it would be better to store the time in a variable and instead each frame check if the current time is different. If so, redraw the clock and update the time variable.

- map() is nice and everything, but why abuse it? The "mapping" for the clock is quite simple. For instance, let secondAngle = sc/60*360;   instead of let secondAngle = map(sc, 0, 60, 360);   and similar for minutes and hours.

- instead of translating and rotating the whole canvas (which could cause confusion if more drawings are added later on), you could set the start angle for all the arcs at -90 degrees. Even better, use let startAngle = -90;  and call arc() using startAngle+secondsAngle as the end angle.

- A fancy way to achieve the clock hands without calling the line() function would be to use PIE in the arc() calls.

CommentText: Tim, echoing what others have noted, it’s crucial to avoid f-strings, simple concatenation, or .format when logging. It's best to use %s or a similar placeholder in your log message, and then provide the variable as an argument to the logging function. For instance: in_val = 105 logging.info('Tip amount entered: %s, exceeds 100 percent', in_val). This prevents unnecessary log message formatting overhead, particularly if the log level is set to error. By passing the variable as an argument, the message formatting is deferred until it’s necessary for output.

VideoTitle: SQL vs NoSQL or MySQL vs MongoDB
CommentText:
Great comparison that gives a clear overview of the two databases structure.


I don't see anyone mention it in the comments. You are kind of technically wrong about one to one relationship between two tables in a SQL database. (@6:13)


In your example you can still have 2 user records pointing to the same contact data record. This can happen if someone updates the table in the database or if there is a bug in your application logic.
What you should have for a true one to one relationship is having both tables having the same id, this means that the PK of contact data table is also the FK to the user table with has PK id as well.
Another approach is to have a unique constraint on the column contact_data_id to ensure that you cannot have multiple contacts with the same value.
In the 2 cases above you would receive an error from the database if you try to add or update a user record with a contact_data_id that is already in use.

VideoTitle: Ukraine Invasion: Foreign Secretary says attacks could be 'beginning of the end' for Putin
CommentText:
The President of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyi, has taken on the role that history has reserved for him. Just a few hours before the Russian invasion, Zelenskyi made a speech to the Russians: 'We know that we do not need war, not cold, not hot, not hybrid. But if your troops attack us and someone tries to take our land from us, our freedom, our children's lives, then we will defend ourselves."

 A David and Goliath set-up has emerged between Russia and Ukraine, with the youthful Zelensky pitted against a botoxed Vladimir Putin. It looks bad for Putin, who understands the importance of symbols. It's a testament to the painstaking work he has put into building his tough-man image. Sometimes Putin poses as a judo pro, sometimes he poses with a tiger. But unlike Zelensky, Putin's courage is only theatre. It was last seen when a coronavirus so badly scared Putin that he hid from the public for months, prompting opposition leader Alexei Navalny to dub Putin 'bunker dad'. Putin's fearfulness is probably the very reason why Ukraine had to be invaded. Putin is not really afraid of a NATO invasion, even though he claimed so in his delusional war speech. Why should he be afraid?

 As Mr Putin himself pointed out, Russia is protected by an awful lot of nuclear missiles. It is democracy that Putin fears. Ukraine must be destroyed, because its success would show the depth of Russia's failure. And that, in turn, could mean a personal moment of reckoning for Putin. In Putin's mind, Ukraine is neither a country nor a nation but a periphery of Russia. Now this periphery is fighting for its freedom. In just a few days, this struggle has already produced heroic stories, such as the defenders of Snake Island who defied a Russian battleship, or the intrepid President in his green T-shirt. The worst thing for Putin is that Zelensky cannot be defeated by killing, for a dead hero will become a legend, just as this war is becoming a prelude to a free Ukraine still emerging from the ruins of war.

 In his old age, Putin is thought to have begun to look for a place for himself in history. He wants to make Russia great again. But history rarely follows plans. Putin may well secure his place in history, but not alongside Peter and Catherine, but alongside Hitler and Stalin, and he may not be remembered as the restorer of Russian greatness, but as the unifier of Ukrainians.

CommentText:
You have to realize that at companies the size of Google, culture is highly dependent on your department or division. I work at a very large tech company and I love my department but we also score extremely high on our employee satisfaction surveys compared to the rest of the company. It's pretty obvious that if I were working in a different part of our tech org, I would not be as happy.

This is just something to keep in mind for people who are new to the tech scene (or really the corporate job scene in general).  It is very important to grill your potential employers when you are interviewing. If one company is offering $150k but you don't get a good feeling from them and another company is offering $130k but you feel like it's a great fit, the second job is going to be a better use of your time and feel more rewarding overall (unless you're a masochist...)

VideoTitle: React Native Tutorial for Beginners - Crash Course 2020
CommentText:
Just wanted to say thanks for this well crafted tutorial.  I work primarily with back end code mainly with Python so this has been very helpful to get my feet wet before jumping into mobile development. 


I also wanted to say something about learning anything regarding programming.  Before I do I want to make sure that everyone understands I'm really not trying to be a dick or put anyone down whatsoever.   This is just something I felt needed saying and I think you'll be better coders for hearing it. 



When you are learning code and you are installing several different libraries and dependencies and languages all of various versions on different operating systems and terminals and IDE's also of various versions you will probably run into a few irritating problems.  Even in a professional environment with programmers who have been working for years will run into unexpected problems that will cause time consuming road blocks.


Which is why this is a perfect time to try and solve these sort of problems your self.  You're going to be doing it at work so you might as well get started doing it during tutorials.  Go to google  or stack overflow and type in the error message you are getting and just see what comes back.  It could be something really easy that looked way worse. 



Being able to troubleshoot and track down random problems like these will prove to be one of your most important skill sets in any career associated with coding.  The tendency in situations like this where a tutorial is involved is to think that someone didn't put in a step that you needed to do before  continue with the tutorial.  But this just isn't the case.  Problems come up all the time in code.  Could be Professional, Hobby or even a Tutorial. 



So before you're quick to judge the situation take a few moments to actually look up the problem that you are seeing.    And you might even be able to post the fix to the group of tutorial watchers who are all complaining about the same thing.   And that'll boost moral like nothing else.    I hope none of this came across the wrong way.  I really did mean all of this to help everyone out.  Best of luck guys!

VideoTitle: HTTP crash course | http Methods | http headers
CommentText: HTTP, or Hypertext Transfer Protocol, serves as the cornerstone for data communication on the World Wide Web. It dictates the formatting and transmission of messages, along with how web servers and browsers should respond to various commands. ### Overview of HTTP 1. **Client-Server Model**: - HTTP operates on a client-server architecture. The client, typically a web browser, initiates requests, while the server, which hosts the website, answers those requests. 2. **Stateless Protocol**: - HTTP is stateless, implying that each client request to the server is independent, and the server retains no memory of prior interactions. ### HTTP Request An HTTP request is initiated by a client toward a server, comprising these elements: 1. **Request Line**: - This includes the HTTP method, the resource URL, and the HTTP version. - Example: `GET /index.html HTTP/1.1` 2. **HTTP Methods**: - **GET**: Used to retrieve data from the server. - **POST**: Sends data for processing to a specified resource. - **PUT**: Updates a resource on the server. - **DELETE**: Removes a resource from the server. - **HEAD**: Similar to GET, but only retrieves HTTP headers without the document body. - **OPTIONS**: Describes the communication options available for the target resource. - **PATCH**: Applies partial modifications to a resource. 3. **Headers**: - These provide extra details about the request or response. Common headers include: - `Host`: Specifies the domain name of the server. - `User-Agent`: Offers details regarding the client software. - `Accept`: Details the media types understandable by the client. - `Content-Type`: Specifies the media type of the resource being sent. - `Authorization`: Contains credentials to authenticate a user-agent with a server. 4. **Body** (Optional): - Used in methods like POST and PUT for sending data to the server. The body may contain various data formats, such as form data or JSON. ### HTTP Response An HTTP response is dispatched by a server to a client, consisting of the following components: 1. **Status Line**: - Includes the HTTP version, a status code, and a status message. - Example: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` 2. **Status Codes**: - These indicate the result of the request. - `1xx`: Informational – Request received, continuing the process. - `2xx`: Success – The action was received, understood, and accepted without issue. - `3xx`: Redirection – Further action is necessary to finalize the request. - `4xx`: Client Error – The request contains incorrect syntax or cannot be completed. - `5xx`: Server Error – The server failed to fulfill a valid request. 3. **Headers**: - Offer additional information about the response. Common headers include: - `Content-Type`: Indicates the media type of the response. - `Content-Length`: Indicates the size of the response body. - `Set-Cookie`: Used to send cookies from the server to the client. 4. **Body** (Optional): - This contains the data requested by the client and can be in formats like HTML, JSON, or an image. ### HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 1. **HTTP/1.1**: - Introduced persistent connections (keep-alive). - Supports multiple requests/responses over a single TCP connection. 2. **HTTP/2**: - Introduces binary framing layer, multiplexing, and header compression. - Enables multiple requests/responses to be in progress simultaneously over a single connection. 3. **HTTP/3**: - Uses QUIC instead of TCP. - Aims to decrease latency and improve performance, particularly in mobile and unstable network environments. ### Security: HTTPS - **HTTPS**: A secure iteration of HTTP that utilizes SSL/TLS to encrypt communication between the client and server. - **SSL/TLS**: Ensures confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. - **Certificates**: Employed to establish secure connections and issued by Certificate Authorities (CAs). ### Common Use Cases 1. **Web Browsing**: - Browsers utilize HTTP to retrieve web pages and resources. 2. **APIs**: - RESTful APIs leverage HTTP methods to execute CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete). 3. **Data Transfer**: - This includes activities like uploading files and submitting form data. Comprehending HTTP is vital for web development, enabling developers to build and troubleshoot web applications, secure communication, and optimize performance.

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge 162: Self-Avoiding Walk
CommentText:
Another way to solve this problem is to use the wave front collapse function, and you can do this quite nicely for any generic graph.

Say you are working with a grid with n dimensions and s_1, s_2, ..., s_n cells in each dimension. As you are moving between the cells of the graph instead of along vertices and edges, if you raise the size of each dimension by 1, then the problem turns into finding a Hamiltonian path on In the case of the slightly larger grid graph / lattice defined by:

G = P_{s_1 + 1} □ P_{s_2 + 1} □ ... □ P_{s_n + 1}

where P_n s the path graph on n vertices and G □ H is the Cartesian / box operator on graphs.

When I was working on the wave front collapse, I made a problem where I used backtracking to find a partitioning of the space of G using wave front collapse. Once the space is partitioned, identifying the connected components is simple and connecting them is just as simple. This results in a Hamiltonian cycle for G, which is also a self-avoiding polygon, and by removing any edge at random, you get a self-avoiding walk. Of course, this limits the problem in some ways, i.e. one of s_n must be odd or it fails (since a Hamiltonian cycle only exists in G if one of the s_n + 1 is even), and it will only give you a specific type of self-avoiding walk (where you start and end one cell apart), but you could probably through some edge flipping get any self-avoiding walk, and the benefit of getting a self-avoiding polygon is a nice extra.


In any case, it's just a fun way to connect two of the problems on this channel. I'm really enjoying the problems here and love your enthusiasm and sense of energy and fun. I love working on random problems to increase my GitHub portfolio and it's also a great way to pick a new language and learn it. (I tend to work in Kotlin most of the time as now that I've gone functional, I can't go back to imperative.)

I usually watch about three or four minutes of one of your videos and then my brain spins out of control and tries to jump ahead to solve the problem before watching the rest of the video, which didn't quite work for my first attempt at wave front collapse.. I did the ASCII art today, which turned out really well, and I'm not convinced that the symbols given are the best for binning the shades of grey, so I'm working on a font analyzer where, given a font with fixed-width glyphs, the algorithm runs over the extended ASCII characters 32 to 255 and determines the percentage of the cell used by the character glyph, and then sorts them and for an integer b of bins that you want (which was 29 in the original problem), returns n-1 characters (since space is obviously the blank character) evenly spaced characters from the densest character to the least dense character to see if that generates a better gray binning colouration. (ChatGPT helped me write the Kotlin code using the java.awt package to do some of the lifting.)

I found for that problem, using the luminance BT.709 gave the best results for combining RGB triples in [0,0xff]^3, which involves mapping the RGB triples to (r, g, b) ∈ [0,1]^3 and then combining them using:

0.2126 * r +  0.7152 * g +  0.0722 * b

to get a grayscale value x ∈ [0,1]. It's quite amazing that blue is considered of so little importance.in this rendering and a pixel's green component is vastly more important than the other values.

In any case, this channel has been a ton of fun and I think that I'm going to start learning Rust and working on the future problems in that.

Thanks for your fantastic videos and all that you do!

VideoTitle: Reverse Linked List - Iterative AND Recursive - Leetcode 206 - Python
CommentText:
The confusing part with his recursive solution is that the base case he calls out is incorrect. The base case he has is actually the edge case when no node is passed into the function. Try throwing in a print statement and you'll see that it's only run when the input is None:
        if not head:
            print('This is the edge case when the input is None')
            return None

Really, the base case is when "head.next == None" (in Python speak "if not head.next"). I rewrote the recursive solution with the base case more apparent:
    def reverseListRecursive(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head:
            print('This is the edge case when the input is None')
            return None

        if not head.next:
            print('This is the base case. At this point, we are at the last node in the list.')
            newHead = head
        else:
            newHead = self.reverseListRecursive(head.next)
            head.next.next = head
            head.next = None

        return newHead

CommentText:
While this is a great productivity tool, it poses some significant dangers to the quality of future software development. 

As developers rely on the automatic code generation capabilities, they will become more and more detached from what the tool actually generates. I can foresee developers simply integrating generated code into system without actually understanding how the code works, and therefore not being able to detect any bugs. Even if the tool is produces top quality code, it will still be dependent on how well the prompt used to produce it was composed. Latent bugs will  get introduced into the codebase, and programmers will have difficulty debugging the code since they don't fully understand it, given that they did not write it. It's the same problem programmers have when attempting to change code written by others - if the programmer doesn't fully understand how the function works they could introduce subtle bugs.

CommentText: This experiment bears little resemblance to real-world conditions. I was the designer of the intake manifold. Here are the key flaws: 1) The cylinders draw in the air-fuel mixture; 2) This happens sequentially, one cylinder at a time; 3) Most importantly, air possesses mass. The larger the turbocharger, the greater the pressure at which it forces air, and consequently, the greater its mass. It is fascinating to observe the shift in gas flow distribution as the turbo reaches operational pressure. Typically, at lower loads, the initial cylinders receive more air in an inline 6-cylinder configuration. However, at higher loads, the final cylinders receive more air due to the gas's mass and energy. While the disproportion is minimal at low loads because the cylinders are SUCKING air, this discrepancy can range from 5-15% at high gas consumption.

CommentText:
Nice Solution. Explanation of the linear time if its not clear right away. 
Though the solution may look like quadratic due to the while loop inside the for loop, the while loop only gets executed at the start of a sequence when (n-1) is not found in the set. Worst case for a sorted array, the first pass will run the while loop (n-1) times, but all other run it will not get executed at all. so the while loop will only run a total of n times for the entire length of the solution. 
so the complexity is O(n+n) which is O(n)..

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge 170: The Monty Hall Problem
CommentText:
People may feel "gotcha"ed, but that's just because the original problem is so vaguely worded.

Switching is ONLY  a superior strategy if the host systematically picks a goat in every game *as a rule*. If instead in every game, the host picks a random unchosen door (so it could be prize or goat), then switching to the remaining door is neither superior nor inferior - and the simple intuition will be correct.

"But the host reveals a goat", some say. But the original problem description is deliberately vague about this: It describes ONE example round, wherein the host reveals an unchosen door, and there is a goat there. And the host knows what is behind the doors. This clever wording leaves you to guess that the host must be using this knowledge to always pick the goat deliberately as a rule of the game (why else would it be mentioned?). But it strictly speaking does not have to be this way.

Of course, if the problem were clearly phrased to begin with, people could just calculate the correct probabilities without ambiguity, and where would the fun be in that!

CommentText: I disagree with the idea of 'separate helper functions' as a general practice. Module-specific helper functions should ideally reside within that module. Similarly, 'unrelated things together' is another way to produce disorder. Also, the one file = one class approach sounds appealing at first but pushes for OOP patterns which is itself problematic.  While not certain what is the best approach, my personal rule is to break things up into modules and files to give single concept to consumers. It is almost the same, but, class is a bad concept approximation. You are more likely to fall into OOP trap if you force concepts into class-shaped boxes.

My dearest hope is that one day, I can discuss cordially with anyone political matters and not have to worry about being insulted or dismissed for my political positions. AI is not ready yet, it's just marketing hype. A processor is quite simple. Considering how many threads your PC handles (hundreds), it is highly improbable that 4 cores will be dedicated solely to your process. You may quickly encounter situations where a streamParallel() call invokes code with its own nested streamParallel(). If the parent uses 4 cores, the child cannot. CommentText:
Pass by value: We pass the copy value of the object and changing the copy of object will not change the original object.

Pass by reference: We pass a reference or memory to the function and changing the object in the function will ultimately change the original object as they both reference to the same memory location.

However in python,
Concept of pass by value or pass by reference is dependent entirely on the mutability of the object passed to the function.

If the passed object is immutable like a number or string. i.e changing them would create entirely new object. Passing by value comes to play.

However in case of mutable objects like lists. Changing the value will cause it to change the original object directly. This feature portrays the pass by reference.

For those who don’t know!:
Pistol shrimp are called as such because they have a special ability. This ability they have is to create areas of high pressure in their larger claw. When they build enough pressure, it sends out something called a “cavitation bubble” these bubbles generate light and heat underwater! They are so full of immense energy and heat they can light up and cause steam underwater. This is their weapon. They use this cavitation bubble they shoot to neutralize or destroy their prey, often opening up the body of the prey due to the large opening created from the blast. From there, they dig right in! The bubbles are small, as are the shrimp, but for anything roughly the same size or smaller than that shrimp, it’s lights out! Edit: for those who want more detail, the cavitation bubble is roughly the same temperature as the surface of our sun. Something so incredible coming from a creature so small. As I said, it creates “openings” on the body. Such as a hole in the stomach, limbs blasted off, you know, the logic of a gun. Just imagine a bullet the temperature of the sun, completely invisible to the naked eye, and moves underwater. This shrimp is also where Clauncher and Clawitzer from Pokemon got their creation ideas from. And yes, the mantis shrimp does similar things. But instead of creating and shooting a cavitation bubble from the palm of its hand, it just throws a punch so hard and so fast cavitation bubbles are a side effect, and create double impacts on their prey.

CommentText: This is a great and simple DIY JavaScript project for beginners. However, technically speaking, try to minimize DOM traversal. VideoTitle: Merge Two Sorted Lists - Leetcode 21 - Python
CommentText:
I had a hard time understanding the dummy..next thing, but finally, I did. Here is my explanation.

Think of the nodes (ListNode) as if each of those was stored in a different memory slot, so each slot has a "next" and a "val" value. So, basically, when you do:

tail = dummy --->  you're creating a tail pointer or reference to where the dummy object is.
then when you do:
tail.next = list1 ----> you're updating the "next" value in the memory slot where the tail is pointing, which is exactly the same slot where dummy is pointing.
then later you do:
tail = tail.next ---> At this point, tail.next is already list1, so you're telling tail to point to the memory slot where list1 is; so if you update later the "next" value of list1, you won't be updating the dummy anymore since tail and dummy are now pointing to different memory slots.

I had to open a Python editor and run the following code to really understand what was happening. id() is a fn that returns a unique memory identifier for the object.

class ListNode:
  def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
    self.val = val
    self.next = next

node1 = ListNode(val=0, next=None)
node2 = node1
print('node1 val', node1.val)
print('node1 next', node1.next)
print(id(node1), id(node2))
print("*****")

node3 = ListNode(val=3, next=None)
print('node1 val', node1.val)
print('node1 next', node1.next)
print(id(node1), id(node2))
print("*****")

node2.next = node3
node2 = node3
print('node1 val', node1.val)
print('node1 next', node1.next.val)
print(id(node1), id(node2))
print("*****")

notes to self:
only combine changes of a single topic in the same commit,

merge: combining two different branches, it creates a merge commit in the process. with merge the two branches keep there own history seperated:
b1-------- c1---------c2-----------------cm
        b2    |----c1-----c2--- c3 -------|
rebase: rebase will unite the two commit histories of both branches, do not use rebase changes pushed to remote repo, rebase diagram:
           before rebase:
           b1:  c1-------------c3------------
           b2    |-------c2-----------c4-----
           after rebase:
           c1-----c2-----c4-----c3*
notice that c3 is at the end, rebase moves commits that happened on b1 after the common ancestor, this means that c3 has changed (different parent)

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge #136.1: Polar Perlin Noise Loops
CommentText:
I was thinking about whether you could make a seamless 2-dimensional texture (there was a video were you used Perlin noise to create a vector field and had particles flow through it, but it had artefacts at the edges where the vector directions would change abruptly).  My first thought was to use the surface of a 3D torus to give a looping 2d texture in the same way you're using the edge of a 2D circle to generate cyclic 1D noise here.  

Then I twigged that the would cause distortion in the texture, since the outer edges of the Torus would sweep through a larger length of the noise pattern than the inner surface for the same angle.  You could minimise it by turning the minor circle so it's tangent to the major circle rather than radial (so your torus would be flattened as if you sucked all the air out of it) but it'd still have a slight distortion to it unless you actually projected the circle onto the surface of a cylinder (sounds complicated, but probably just needs the coordinate calculations to come in the right order).

Part of me wonders if it would be simpler just to write a Perlin noise class that interpolates smoothly between the edges, but that would limit the scale of the noise to integer fractions of the screen space, and might cause issues if you wanted to create images with odd aspect ratios.

VideoTitle: Two Sum - Leetcode 1 - HashMap - Python
CommentText:
I have extensive experience in implementing and operating key:value patterns across a wide spectrum, ranging from custom hash functions to simple Kafka partitioning.
It's been a while since I refreshed my understanding of such problems, so I've started practicing on platforms like LeetCode.
I recognize that while this may seem like a straightforward problem, it took me some time to grasp the logic behind the reverse key:value pattern solution.
I'm sharing my perspective for those already familiar with hash logic (key:value) to potentially aid in understanding such problems in a more generic manner.

Let's disregard the value:index relationship and focus solely on the key:value pattern. In any hash-based operation, the goal is to find a key to return the associated result (value/s). In our scenario, during iterations, we're searching for a value (a number). This means that the value becomes the key in our hash map, and we obtain a result based on the problem's description, which happens to be the 'index' or the key of our original array.

In any problem, the objective is to search for one or more keys and obtain a result. In our case, the crucial aspect is that the result should correspond to the 'old' keys.
So in any scenario where you're utilizing a hash map, your primary focus is on what you're searching for and what the desired result should be.

VideoTitle: Pregnancy Update Q&A | Pregnancy After Miscarriage 🌈
CommentText: Elsa, I was a young hippie chick in 1979 when I had my 1st daughter and I could not relate to the need for acquiring a lot of baby stuff and we had little money. I had picked up a little sweater at Goodwill and a cool Goosy riding toy (I still have) that I thought was neat. When my first daughter, Samala, was born early, my midwife & friend brought a box of onesies and enough little shirts & diapers to get me started. She was born in our apartment totally naturally. Other mothers donated their babies hand me downs. In earlier centuries, moms didn’t need so many things. It was amazing the clothes my daughters acquired from friends with babies. BTW, before I had a baby I had hang ups about my small breasts, but I managed to nurse all 3 of my girls absolutely fine, 2 of them 1 1/2 yrs and the final daughter went till she was 4, more a less a bonding thing. I loved nursing. Having had small breasts that nursed well, they eventually went back to being small again, which I always liked. I too live small, in a Tiny house and I keep it cleaner & more organized than anywhere I have ever lived. I also have a 13’ Scamp. I love having small spaces now, easier to clean & uncluttered. I so look forward to seeing you all enjoying parenthood and I love that you are finding peace in being so chill with this process. All 3 of my girls were natural births and yet each time I so looked forward to the pregnancies, last one I was 37 yrs old. My grandson is expecting with his partner very close to your time. I cannot believe I will be a great Nana soon. Thanks for being so transparent so others can learn from your openness. Simpler living is something we can all benefit from, less debt, more time to enjoy what we have. You guys got this!

CommentText: Jeff, with all due respect, that's a completely unfounded detour. We have retail Steam games with data discs here, or at least did until very recently. The decompression for those was pretty much as CPU-intensive as Steam downloads at the time, for similar reasons - the DVD drives aren't fast and more uncompressed data needs more DVDs (and more swaps), plus the CPU isn't doing much else when a gamer wants to play so might as well use it. And this wasn't only on Steam games; older PC game installers did the same thing. Even PlayStation installations do this despite dedicated decompression circuits. Discs have benefits sometimes, but they don't eliminate the intense computing for installation decompression.

VideoTitle: Is Coding Still Worth Learning in 2024?
CommentText: The idea of prompt engineering is overhyped, and here's the reason: People mistakenly believe that instructing an AI is straightforward because you just write in simple English and it's solved. But natural English is too ambiguous. That's why programming languages exist. They exist solely to tell a machine what to do unambiguously with consistent results. If you simply describe what you want to an AI in plain English, it may seem fine initially, but the AI might interpret things differently than you intended, which you may only discover when a large transaction is happening. Therefore, plain English is not adequate for writing code. The creators of Python attempted to solve this, but they essentially created another programming language.

CommentText: It's truly engaging to observe someone tackle these challenges. I greatly appreciate how you navigate the entire process from start to end, without removing the iterations, the working through each logical step, the experiments, errors and learning from them.  However, one thing is somewhat painful to watch, since it makes me feel bad that you're having to do everything the hard way. The number of issues that you encounter because you're a human and it's impossible to keep every detail in your conscious focus illustrates a lot, and highlights the advantages of utilizing a strongly-typed language. For example, with F#, almost all of these minor "gotcha" situations would have been prevented because, when written idiomatically, and if you create types that are only correct when everything is correct, the compiler will verify all logic interacting with those types and will not allow incorrect code to build.  I'm so grateful I don't have to work in JavaScript. However, this is not criticism of you; I enjoy these videos immensely and they are exceptionally helpful in learning how to dissect complex problems into manageable steps. You're a great educator and enjoyable to watch. I just feel bad that the compiler doesn't give you the needed support for simple human error.

CommentText:
It’s interesting how common sense can differ across cultures. What might seem like an obvious reaction like keeping your kids safe and secure in an emergency can be elevated to “expert advice” in some places, while in others, it’s just an instinctive response.

The way certain advice is received often reflects deeper cultural differences. In many foreign countries, survival instincts and situational awareness are taught from a young age, either out of necessity or cultural practice. Meanwhile, in parts of the U.S., there’s a heavier reliance on professionals or systems to guide behavior in crises. It’s not necessarily bad it’s just a different approach to preparedness and self-reliance.

What’s amusing is how something universally practical can be hailed as “revolutionary” when delivered in a certain context. It’s almost like the packaging of the message matters more than the content. Do you think this points to a broader issue of over-complicating simple solutions in some cultures? Or maybe it’s a reflection of how certain societies are conditioned to rely more on external expertise?
America can do better.

VideoTitle: React.js vs Angular vs Vue
CommentText: In my opinion, React functions more as a library than a framework. For smaller projects, React works perfectly well. However, because it relies heavily on third-party libraries, you'll have to invest time to find the right fit for your needs, which can lead to inconsistencies in coding style. This can cause issues as your project grows. The React library only provides essential app-building tools. You can essentially build your own framework with React. For an extensible app, Angular is the best choice, as it offers everything required to build a robust, scalable app, including end-to-end and unit testing. If you plan to hand off the project to colleagues, Angular helps you write better code through concepts like MVVM (MVC). While React can do this as well, you'll need additional libraries or frameworks. Furthermore, with Angular 7 onwards, the rendering is superb. So I would suggest Angular for developers who want clean, scalable, and well-tested code, while React is preferable for those with strong web backgrounds who enjoy writing their own libraries and frameworks. Why Angular? For example, if Android gets new hardware information, Google's Angular team will probably be the first to get that information, making it more compatible with cutting-edge technologies.

CommentText: Two things, first I am a native Californian and have been around for 68 years now. During that time I have seen, witnessed, and fought brush fires in So. Cal. When I was in high school from ‘70-‘74, I took science classes. The last was oceanography. Our teacher warned us about a growing trend called “global climate change”. He also had copies of reports as far back as the early 1800’s of “cataclysmic” climate change being predicted and that those changes would destroy all life on earth, destroy the earth, either the planet would be covered in ice or become a planet like mars, etc.. Every year, usually between late October through March, we get to experience Santa Ana winds. When I lived in Ontario from ‘72-‘78, the winds would howl through southeast Ontario sometimes (gusts) at over 100 miles per hour and sustained winds of 35 mph. “Climate change” has nothing to do with it, it’s been happening here for hundreds of years. Second, I have noticed that every time So. Cal. suffers through these winds, the media starts reporting about the lower humidity and the winds and the heightened fire danger. I understand why this is done but I have also noticed that every time these warnings go out, the fires begin. On Dec. 2nd, 1990, I was a working at a federal facility near Pasadena. During the early evening, I was dispatched to a fence alarm on east perimeter of the facility. I noticed a male subject walking on the outside of the fence line and holding onto the fence to keep from falling into the dry riverbed. He then lowered himself into the 5ft. tall weeds and started walking in a circle then took out a book of matches, struck one match then lit the whole book. It was at this time that my supervisor and I yelled at him to stop what he was doing and stand still. He complied and we were able to detain him for local L.E.. We later found out that he was a “walk away” from a mental facility for criminals. He was a serial arsonist and had heard about the heightened fire danger, walked out of the facility (staff paying attention?), walked east toward the riverbed and was going to set the area of Altadena and La Canada on fire. It doesn’t take a “rocket scientist “ to figure out that there a plethora of these folks just waiting to hear about the wind or fire danger to kickstart their nefarious activities. Just an observation that I felt compelled to share. Just my opinion.

VideoTitle: Vanilla CSS vs Bootstrap vs Tailwind CSS - Which one should you choose?
CommentText: I think this video misunderstands Tailwind's strengths and weaknesses in common practice. First, pretty much everyone who uses Tailwind in production also uses PurgeCSS to remove unused code/classes. This is such a common thing that the Tailwind people put the PurgeCSS set-up instructions in their own docs. Second, you do have a lot of control with Tailwind because every class is easily customized, you can easily add your own Tailwind-ed classes, etc. But with that said, some lack of control in Tailwind is intended because it's a tool for creating design systems. Having only nine shades of blue or only ten padding options is the whole point. This kind of limited, curated set of choices helps you create fast, cohesive, consistent designs across your site. Third, I would argue against the idea that no expert knowledge of CSS is needed to use Tailwind. For example, one of Tailwind's greatest strengths is how it handles responsive breakpoints, but I think it would be difficult to use these classes well without in-depth understanding of CSS media queries. Tailwind is weird in that you write no CSS but probably need to know a lot about CSS to use it effectively.

def fibDPTabulation(position):
    if position <= 1: return 1
    table = list()
    table = [0 for i in range(0, position+1)]
    table[1] = 1
    
    length = len(table)
    for i in range(2, length):
        table[i] = table[i-2] + table[i-1]
    
    return table[position]

VideoTitle: Being an Introvert is a Good Thing. | Crystal Robello | TEDxStMaryCSSchool
CommentText:
I'm here today trying to be something I'm not.
Which is something I've been trying to do for two years now:
write a TED Talk, share my ideas,
talk in front of such a large group of people.
I know a lot of you are probably thinking, "She sounds a bit shy."
Or maybe, "She probably gets nervous easily."
Yeah, all those things are 100% true, but why?

To answer simply, I am an introvert.
So what is an introvert?
An introvert is a quiet person that doesn't like to talk very much
and likes to keep their thoughts mostly to themselves.
They're the kind of person that goes home just to relax and have time to think.
But that's not to say that an outgoing person can't be an introvert.
Just as long as they enjoy the quiet time to get to themselves,
they're most likely an introvert to a certain extent.
So the main thing I want to address in this talk
is that there's nothing wrong with being an introvert.
However society doesn't see it in the same lighting.
Society has taught us that being an introvert is the worst thing you can be
and that everyone should want to be extroverted.
We're told that being outgoing is good and being shy and quiet is bad.

We're told in elementary school we have to raise our hands,
participate in class or we lose marks.
Every year at parent-teacher interviews, my parents would hear the same thing,
"Your daughter is very shy, she needs to learn to speak up more."
I was told to share my voice whenever possible.
As an introvert, those are some very hard standards to achieve.
This is why I joined the TED Ed Club two years ago -
to prove to not only myself but to everyone that I wasn't shy.
I could write a talk just like everyone else is doing it.
No big deal.
Slight problem, I never wrote a talk.
I couldn't come up with a topic I was truly passionate about
that I felt like I wanted to share with the world.
I would show up to every meeting
and watch my peers continue to develop their talks
and I would get frustrated with myself.
Why could they share their ideas so easily and I couldn't even come up with a topic?
Now, looking back, I realize I have passions,
I have views on the world and I have opinions.
I just didn't want to share any of them because I'm an introvert.

But is there anything wrong with that?
Statistics say that 50% of the American population is made up of introverts.

So society is telling 50% of Americans - about 160 million people -

that they need to change who they are
to be accepted, to be successful and to be happy.
Keep in mind,
within this large group of introverts are people such as:
Elton John, Emma Watson, Michael Jordan, Audrey Hepburn, Albert Einstein,

and so many more incredible, inspiring people.

Do you think being an introvert has ever stopped any of them
from achieving their goals or being happy?
No.
A lot of you have probably been told something along the lines
of why be a follower when you can be a leader.
But what about every leader needs a follower?
Let's look at Mr. Justin Trudeau, Prime Minister of Canada.
Do you think he'd be where he is today without the support of the people?
If everyone was trying to be a leader no one would truly succeed
as it's the followers that define a true leader.
But that's not to say that an introvert can't be a leader.
Let's look at Abraham Lincoln, Rosa Parks and Gandhi.
All incredible inspirational leaders and all introverts.

In a business setting,
the CEO of a company will look at an introvert and say,
"If they're not going to share their ideas they are useless to me."
Well, guess what?
These companies are missing out.
Introverts are known to be versatile, responsible,
work well in small groups and individually.
So being an introvert has no effect on how happy
or how successful you are going to be
as long as you see it in the right lighting.
If you see yourself as an introvert
and think it's the worst thing in the world,
you're never going to be truly happy with yourself
and you're going to constantly try to change to conform to society.
But if you accept yourself as an introvert and you're happy,
there's nothing in the way
of you achieving your goals and getting what you want.
All in all, there is absolutely nothing wrong with being an introvert.
No matter what society may say,
you don't need to change who you are because being an introvert is great.
Before I leave, I want to end with a quote from the book "Quiet,
The power of introverts in a world that can't stop talking"
by Susan Cain.
"The secret to life is to put yourself in the right lighting.
For some, it's a Broadway spotlight; for others, it's a lamplit desk."

So the next time you see that quiet kid in the back of the class
who doesn't participate very much,
I want you to think,
"I wonder what great things they're going to come up with next."
Thank you.

CommentText: Seeing a lot of people being worried about the screws being easily pulled out. While it's not ideal it isn't as bad as it seems. The direction of the force on the screws due to a fall would put pressure on the screw such that it will pivot around the front bottom of the screw cavity. This would raise the back end of the screw and jam it into the top back of the cavity. The screw threads will then help keep it stuck in the ice whereas a perpendicular force away from the wall would be easy if the cavity is wider than the screw threads.

VideoTitle: I Dropped Out Of Computer Science
CommentText:
I went the traditional route for the most part and got a computer science degree. However, during the time that I was going to school, I found jobs in my field. I started working as a QA (someone who manually tests code after a new feature or bug has been fixed), then worked my way into a QA Automation (where you write automated tests -- so you actually get to write code) but still offer a lot of manual support as needed for regular QAs, some really simple software freelance work up until I got my first full-time position as an associate software engineer. While going to school is a great way to learn and get better qualified for a job, a lot of my path has included a lot of getting actual work experience in my field while going to school. The point being that on-the-job training is really essential (in my opinion) to really learn the field and to build up a resume to get hired easier.

A college degree is not the only way to get into a software engineering job. It's possible to work your way into that field by starting out as a QA, and working your way up to it. It may require you to change jobs multiple times (the company you may not have all the opportunities to move up -- and I changed jobs multiple times while I was working into positions that eventually led me to be a software engineer). If you don't do college, learning is still essential. And while coding bootcamps can help give someone a jump start into learning something, most of the time, you'll probably not get a job right out of a coding bootcamp. Even after college, you still need to be always learning. Computer science is very technical, and some people want to get into it because it's glamorized and realize they hate it because they hate working at a very technical level. The best software engineers I've worked with are those who are typically working on side projects at home and who are always learning. They're the ones that move up. I've also interviewed software engineer candidates who are fresh graduates with a degree but who have not spent a lot of time outside of the time learning in school or on the job who have not done well at all. I've also interviewed candidates with no degree or who did a coding bootcamp who knew their stuff, had great initiative and who were greater employees later on.

The point is, don't just get a college degree because it's "guaranteed." It's a great way to learn and show potential employers that you've learned the skills needed to start doing the job. However, I'm against going to extremely high end colleges both because they're way too expensive with not enough payout (it's a horrible money choice) and because they have the mentality that you should spend all your time working on massive class projects when your time would really be much better spent going to a simple college close to home for much cheaper and getting work experience on the side. Dream colleges (or Ivy League, or whatever other prestigious college is being pushed) are just a way to take massive amounts of money on vague promises of elite wealth.

Long story short, you don't need college to be a software engineer, but you absolutely need to really love writing, debugging, and reading through code, and need to spend plenty of time on your own learning (even if you've been in the field 20 years), and being able to prove to potential employers you have these skills (either through building a website, youtube channel, github, etc) or by working your way up from QA into software engineering.

            nums[l] = nums[r]

CommentText:
I used to sail with my dad as a kid to different islands off the northwest coast, hiking the islands and exploring...and as you may know, kids seem to find the best times to have to poop, so the journey began, a search for a suitable place for me to leave my little mark on this earth. We walked and walked and walked and finally, I thought it was over, it was either going to be my pants or the plants, but then suddenly, we made it through to an opening, where lo and behold, we had found probably thee one and only lonely outhouse that existed on this island! "Hope had been found! Hallelujah!", I thought. Of course, at this very moment my sphincter was nearly flaccid, no strength left whatsoever... so I walked over to the outhouse, up the step or two, and as a good young lad would, I knocked... cordially..., only to be met with an earnest reply... "I'll be right out!", she said. This was the greatest and worst news I could have received. The good news is they would "be out soon", but the 
fact that someone answered, where literally no one was to be found, experiencing the same anguish as myself. I'll never forget that moment, or how hard my dad was laughing, with me, at me, with them afterward, and later in life. Thanks outhouse girl, wherever you are, for one of the funniest memories of my life.

VideoTitle: Why "Democratic" Socialism Doesn't Work
CommentText:
I'm pretty sure Denmark came out to refute Bernie's claim that they were socialist...

Welfare is welfare, and capitalism is not anarchy where you're all on your own.

Denmark is/was closer to capitalism, because just like how you can't have capitalism without a free market, you can't have socialism without a totalitarian, centrally controlled economy, but a social security net for when you CAN'T provide for yourself isn't socialism.

It depends on how much of society is subsidised, and you start getting close when you can have living arrangements, food and entertainment all without contributing in any way despite not being in need of such financial aid.

Under capitalism, the individual is incentivised to contribute his labour: either starting his own production or working and getting paid by his employer (who himself contributes by letting his employees get an agreed upon amount for helping him use the facilities that he either built or bought to produce a good), this money being proof that he has contributed to society and how much (based on how much the community values his product or service, measured by supply and demand), and he then buys things that another person has in surplus using this same proof of contribution, letting the producer in turn buy something else with this proof of contribution.

Of course, without a centrally planned economy, different things will be worth more or less, based not upon the wisdom of the enlightened leader, but on supply and demand, which means not everything is within everyone's buying range.

He is however not consigned to eternally keep working for someone who doesn't pay well enough, or even working for someone else at all, but can under a free market save up and obtain his own means of production by being thrifty, and if things go well, eventually hire employees of his own to grow the company, which will only prosper as much as the community wants his goods or services.

CommentText: The background checks, at least in Tennessee, seem to be incredibly sensitive in my experience. I went to purchase my first firearm, a 9mm handgun (brand new), and was denied. I thought that may have been due to filling out the paperwork incorrectly since I wrote something on the wrong line, asked the seller (certified firearm dealer) what to do and they instructed me to just mark out what I wrote and rewrite on the correct line. Since I felt weird about botching the paperwork I let it go and just tried again somewhere else much much later (months I think). This time I went to a different dealer, filled out the paperwork correctly and was denied again .. I waited for my denial letter, which effectively explained nothing so I went straight to the local police department to see if they knew anything I didn't. They confirmed I had no record, no outstanding tickets or court fines. Nothing. I spoke to some private investigators in that same office and they were appalled at the situation. They said sometimes (somehow) they mix applicants up based on their names (which is wild bc .. your social security number is on the application ..) but my name is incredibly unique, as they stated. Both my first and last name are .. odd 😅 like you can google my first name and I'm the first thing that pops up 💀 so anyway .. I appealed the TICS decision, waited weeks for a response, tried again and BINGO. Finally .. my first firearm 🎉

VideoTitle: Alexa and Google... It's Inevitable
CommentText:
Loving the Shelly devices, having used many other home automation systems and being a software dev, the connectivity and functionality they have really impresses me. It's noticeable that theirs a very common UI and code base between the different devices, which is really nice, I'm phasing out my SmartThings setup and moving over to Shelly for all my home automation stuff now.

I've got a bunch of PM4s running in an industrial unit for nearly a year now, they're working great, they are configured and work in the same easy way the sockets are, I've got energy monitors on the incoming power as well, also fantastic, door contact sensors on 3D printer doors, the power goes through the a Shelly socket so power is switched on if the door is opened (i.e. taking a finished print off the bed ready for the next one), I have a Home Assistant routine that triggers when the power usage drops below 10W for 20 minutes (an indication the 3D printer has finished printing), which powers off the printer, this has been incredibly reliable (impressive that the device can measure upto 3kw, but also measure and be stable measuring just a few watts.

Suggest setting the Input/Output settings to 'Restore the last mode it was in, when it has power' - I found one device with poor WiFi connectivity kept switching off, which I think was because it lost WiFi, and then for whatever reason, did its power on routine when it got WiFi back, which sets the socket to Off. Powering up in the Off state is obviously the safest option, but can catch you out (it has me numerous times!).


The functionality of the BLE devices (i.e. door contact) is sadly very limited, even though you can use the sockets as a gateway for them, doing anything interesting with them outside the shelly system is difficult.

The ApplianceType options for power usage allocation in the Shelly cloud is sadly limited (hoping I can add custom ones one day, maybe I've just not found the right place).

Shelly should totally send you a load more of their stuff to do more great videos like this one! I get most of my Shelly devices through ShellyStore (.co.uk), might be worth reaching out to them.

VideoTitle: Laravel From Scratch | 4+ Hour Course
CommentText:
Amazing course, thank you Traversy Media! I'm being transparent about this course though. I'm new to the backend world and just know the basics of javascript and how the DOM in javascript works as a scope of my knowledge with a coding language. However, I got to the database section and felt super overwhelmed trying to understand where/what connects to what and what everything is doing through this laravel application. So, I started the course completely over. So, the second time around, I literally went through each section Trasversy Media covers and once he covered it, I would pause the video and write down the code, name, and a short meaning of what he covered, and that helped me tremendously! I HIGHLY recommend that for any newbie developer that's coming into the tech space or learning PHP/laravel for the first time. The reason why I suggest it is because it doubles your learning by soaking it in from doing the course along with Trasversy Media but also writing it down gives you clarity, explaining what that snippet of code is doing as well as the name of it. And lastly, redoing what you just got taught from your brain and no notes will test you on the syntax as well as you developing the skill of talking things out loud to solve the problem.

PS: I hope this message reaches future developers trying to learn Laravel! I know you can do it, just remind yourself. If you can build laravel applications that immediately give you the permission to ask for at least $60k at any company, and for most of us that is life-changing and from there it only increases even higher for you. So, just endure this short-term struggle now, and afterward, you'll reap the rewards of your hard work and success!🙌😃

VideoTitle: The Most Popular Programming Languages & Their Uses (2020)
CommentText:
This video is very well done. Well-scripted. Well-presented. Factually accurate. Kudos.

Of this list, my favourite is Go. I've used JavaScript, Python, Java, and C++, and I don't like any of them. I understand *why* they are popular (strong libraries, plentiful job opportunities), but none of them are pleasant to use.

JavaScript is a very sloppy and undisciplined language full of potholes and dark corners. Python, while easy to learn, is not much better.

Java feels like a straightjacket and C++ is mind-numbingly complicated.

That said, my favourite programming language, bar none, is Smalltalk. While it's not very popular, it has enormous advantages:

- Smalltalk is very, very simple and easy to learn (much more so than Python) — the complete syntax fits on a post card!
- Thus, Smalltalk imposes a virtually nonexistent cognitive load on the programmer.
- Smalltalk is the purest and most elegant of OOP languages. This makes writing large, scalable systems relatively painless.
- By using TDD, Smalltalk is safe, reliable, and maintainable.
- Smalltalk's image-based development system offers many benefits — it's comparable to containerized software like Docker.
- Smalltalk is the most productive programming language — you can typically write a Smalltalk application in a fraction of the time it would take in Python, JavaScript, and Java.
- Smalltalk is extremely flexible and versatile — it can be used for web, AI, data science, IoT, VR/AR, enterprise, etc.

I love this language to pieces. For more information, visit smalltalk.tech.blog.

The `if` statement assesses `!username`'s result. If it's `true` (meaning `username` is falsy), the code within the `if` block executes. Essentially, `if (!username)` checks if `username` is either missing (`undefined`) or an empty string (`''`), executing the code inside the `if` block if so. If `username` has any other value, the `if` block is skipped."

CommentText: I'm not sure why the explanation covers cases where nothing is added to the array. It seems like alternating between adding and skipping an element each time would be both faster and possibly easier for some to grasp. I'm sharing my implementation below in case it's useful to anyone. class Solution { public: vector<vector<int>> combinationSum(vector<int>& candidates, int target) { vector<vector<int>> result; vector<int> subset; DFS(result, subset, candidates, target, 0, 0); return result; } private: void DFS(vector<vector<int>>& result, vector<int>& subset, const vector<int>& candidates, int target, int sum, int index) { if (sum >= target) { if(sum == target) { result.push_back(subset); } return; } for(int i = index; i < candidates.size(); i++) { subset.push_back(candidates[i]); DFS(result, subset, candidates, target, sum + candidates[i], i); subset.pop_back(); } } };

print(nlp2("fries").similarity(nlp2("hamburgers"))) = .58
print(nlp2("fries").similarity(nlp2("ham burgers"))) = .70
print(nlp2("french fries").similarity(nlp2("hamburgers"))) = .46
print(nlp2("french fries").similarity(nlp2("ham burgers"))) = .64

Also, I find that the small model correctly identifies West Chestertenfieldville as a GPE without modification, and I find that nlp.add_pipe("entity_ruler") does not add of the pipeline-description we see via nlp.analyze_pipes(). I suspect this does not say anything about the true order of the pipeline.

CommentText:
Should we use PQ or quickSelect in this problem?  PQ seems inefficient because first we have to insert all the items from array into PQ(maxHeap), then we have to extract the max/root 'k' times and finally we get answer. And every time we perform insertion or extraction the heap has to readjust itself via heapifyUp or heapfiyDown respectively. 
This leads me to believe quickSelect is more desirable for this problem.

CommentText:
Copyright and IP are dying concepts. What does IP or Copyright mean in a future where everything is created by an AI and where anyone else could reproduce the same thing with a single prompt? I think we're going to have to let go of those concepts. AI also means we need a new economic model, what we have no simply won't work. It would lead to a dystopian nightmare. Think about it: AI is only ever going to get better, faster, cheaper. And it's going to compete in the workforce for jobs. This means human salaries will plummet to near zero over time, but your debt will remain the same. The wealth gap would also widen irreparably. A new economic model is needed in this type of post-labor economy. Hopefully leaders around the world are putting their heads together to come up with something that will be equitable and fair for all. We have a chance to do it right this time. Money no longer needs to be the driving force in the future. Instead, people can focus on what really matters, finding meaning in their lives and helping others. It's just like we see in retirement, they go through stages:
1. Joy as they explore their lifelong dreams
2. Boredom when they realize those dreams were hollow and unfulfilling
3. Search for meaning - exploring hobbies, visiting family and friends, helping others, exploration, etc. This is the final stage for those with a successful retirement.
4. Those that either didn't do step 3, or who couldn't get outside of themselves fall into this stage - listlessness. They seek ways to make the clock spin faster and return to work to fill their lives with empty drudgery because that's all they know that can pass the time. In a post-labor economic future, they could still do this. They just wouldn't get paid.

If it goes right, for example, and gets stuck it backtracks to the left, but right is once again a valid option.  Therefore, it's possible to always choose right, get stuck, backtrack to the left, choose right, ad infinitum.  You need to have a list of attempts from each point, so when it backtracks it can't try an attempted option again, so it backtracks further once all attempts from that point on the current path are taken, if it reverts and comes to that point again, it's on a new path, therefore all options are once again valid.

CommentText:

RT won't make sense until it can be run with almost no performance penalty. VideoTitle: Math isn't hard, it's a language | Randy Palisoc | TEDxManhattanBeach
CommentText: I remember while in school that i found math to be the vain of my existence (I love science, including the more math based forms, but never figured i could get it). 11 years of schooling went by with me detesting and dreading going to math classes. Then i took an elective called Fundamentals of Technology during my junior year in highschool. This class was in essence an applied physics class with math, math, and more math. The difference was that it was just that, applied math. I wasnt figuring out some undetailed single math problem, i was solving formulas with a story behind them. I was taking a rocket and firing the engines at full blast and figuring out that the Force was equal to the mass times its acceleration. You often here people use the expression "Its not rocket science" but in this case that is exactly what it was. My teacher ended up teaching 4 of my courses before i graduated highschool and turned out to be a great mentor and good friend because he was able to look at the world and not just explain that it spun like my other math teachers for 11 previous years did, but showed me why it spun and that changes your outlook on math. I went from one of the lowest scoring students in my class for math to one of the top scoring students in 1 semester. I broke through the barrier of seeing math as something foreign by seeing how it connects in the real world. I took meaningless problems from my real math courses and made my own analogies for their meaning. A lot of times it really only comes down to a good teacher, someone who doesnt tell you that something is what it is, but explains why it is like it is. Thank you Mr. Morris.

If u have inverter AC which most likely to be a case these days, don't turn it on and off again and again, set it on a comfortable temperature for longer hours. 
AC compressor consumes more current during start up, but if it runs on same speed for longer hours it consumes little current. 
It's like your vehicle consumes more fuel in city where u accelerate and apply brakes more frequently; but the vehicle consumes less fuel on highways where you keep it running on same speed.
Normal ac turns off and on its compressor as per the thermostat, but inverter AC doesn't turn the compressor off, it sets its speed as per the desired temperature and keep it running on the set speed, as a result it consumes less current while maintaining the desired temperature for long hours.

VideoTitle: Combination Sum - Backtracking - Leetcode 39 - Python
CommentText:
We could optimize this solution by sorting nums and stopping recursion if prev element in sorted array itself didn't add up to result

For this example
candidates = [2,3,6,7], target = 7

The usual dfs solution will trace in the below way

2 - 2 - 2 - 2(8 > target) so return
2 - 2 - 2 - 3
2 - 2 - 2 - 6
2 - 2 - 2 - 7
After completing the above pattern only it will move one level up

2 - 2 - 3(7 == target) 
if you notice in the first pattern,
already adding up index - 0 which is 2 makes the target bigger
Why do we need to go down on the sorted array by trying the next larger nos?

Thus breaking that level will save considerable time

Complete Code:

def combinationSum(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
        n = len(nums)
        nums.sort()
        results = []
        subset = []
    
        def dfs(target, index):
            if target == 0:
                results.append(subset.copy())
                return

            for i in range(index, n):
                new_target = target - nums[i]
                
				if new_target >= 0:
                    subset.append(nums[i])
                    
					dfs(new_target, i)
                    
					subset.pop()
                else:
                    return

        dfs(target, 0)
        return results

VideoTitle: What is MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) Pattern?
CommentText: In terms of testing, it appears you focus on end-to-end or integration tests while neglecting unit tests. A disadvantage of this approach is that you may have to develop significant amounts of code before being able to test anything. With end-to-end testing, you need to build the entire system before testing. As a consequence, it may become difficult to catch errors early, potentially leading to wasted development time on a broken application. Another drawback is that identifying the broken code when bugs arise will be challenging. With unit tests, you can easily pinpoint which system component is faulty, and you can do that earlier in the development cycle.

VideoTitle: Dynamic Programming - Learn to Solve Algorithmic Problems & Coding Challenges
CommentText:
Great tutorial, but I believe you missed something in the grid traveler problem. You correctly observed that whenever one of the dimensions is 0, the answer will always be 0. But, similarly, when either of the dimensions is 1, the answer will always be 1, so you don't have to continue the recursion until it reaches a case of (1,1) as it is quite literally a bunch of unnecessary steps. Whether it's (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 100), or (1, 9999999), there will always be only one way. So, I would make the base case be:
if either of the dimensions is 1, return 1.
If either is 0, return 0. 
This can easily be observed from the tree you drew as well.

I know that, generally, this doesn't change much, but it would speed up the code a lot for edge cases such as (1, 999999999999).

VideoTitle: C Programming Tutorial for Beginners
CommentText:
For people still confused on Pointers, I thought of a little analogy:

Say your friend wants to know where you live. Think of your hometown as memory, with lots of houses being stored (variables), and addresses to locate them (pointers). You wouldn't show your friend, say, a picture of your house and expect them to find it quickly. Therefore, you would give your friend your house's address (a pointer), so they can locate it easily.

Now, let's put it to proper terms.

C wants to know what the variable you're referring to is. You have memory, with lots of variables being stored, and addresses to locate them. You can't give C your variable name and expect C to find it amongst all of your other variables, so you refer to its address as a pointer so C can easily locate it.

Hope this helped :)

Edit: thanks for all the love this comment got <3. realised this isnt the most technical analogy (wrote it when i was 15, im nearly 18 now 😅) so to further it:

showing your friend a picture of your house, as opposed to the address is analogous to showing C a variable name (which it sees as the variable's value) as opposed to the variable address (a pointer).

    *translate(width/2, height/2);*  // move the origin to the center of the canvas

        The map that Dan retrieves are based on the longitude and latitude as (0, 0).
        In the real world, all longitude and latitude values (positive/negative) 
        are referred based on location (0, 0).

   /* imageMode(CENTER) interprets the second and third parameters of image() 
        as the image's center point. If two additional parameters are specified, 
        they are used to set the image's width and height. */

    *image(worldMapImage, 0, 0);*
    /* Because of CENTER mode, the (0, 0) indicates the center of the image.
       And due to translate(width/2, height/2),  (0, 0) is at the center of the Canvas. */

Listening to her speak…or should I say “act” is a telling sign as well. It’s very difficult to get up and speak in front of someone who abused you. Does Johnny punch walls and slam cabinet doors….sure….does he pass out on the couch….sure….but those things aren’t evidence of physical abuse.
