CommentText:
I know this is an older video and I think you had something like this on the whiteboard at one point but I'm not sure it was fully explained about how the weights/inputs and lines are related. So if anyone is confused hopefully this helps?

You can take the equation for a line you probably learned in school: y = mx + b and rearrange it into this form:  

0 = mx - y + b

m is the slope of the line which we can say is m=rise/run. So:

0 = (rise/run)x - y + b

Then if we multiply everything by run we get this:

0 = run(rise/run)x - y(run) + b(run), which simplifies to
0 = x(rise) - y(run) + b(run)

But rise, -run and b(run)  are all just arbitrary numbers so call them p, q and r. Then the general equation for a line is:

0 = px + qy + r(1)   

Obviously the multiplication r(1) could just be r but it shows how everything is related: The inputs are x, y and 1 with the coefficients p, q and r being the weights. So a simple perceptron models a line because it's essentially a function which computes the points on a line. Or more specifically, the points (x, y) such that the right-hand side equals zero are on the line, points where the value is negative are on one side of the line and points where the value is positive are on the other.

(Apologies if I'm being overly pedantic here. I think you did—and in general on all your videos, do—a great job explaining potentially confusing topics in an easy to understand way. VideoTitle: I Dropped Out Of Computer Science
CommentText:
Pretty crazy I started watching you as a dirt broke college student, when I decided that computer science was something I wanted to take seriously. Working at u-haul and living off ramen, loans and caffeine. You seemed so on top of your craft. Now I'm a homeowner and spend my time tinkering with pet projects and working in a really cool swe job that doesn't even really feel like a job, even in crunch times.

I stuck out my college degree, and I regret it. It was wasted time, learning about things like data structures, basic algorithms, compilers and all that was useful but it was taught with extremely archaic technologies by predominantly old people who were completely oblivious to how much the world has passed their knowledge by, and were totally unwilling to listen to feedback to update anything.

Most of what I learned was useless. Totally useless. I realized this 2 and a half years in, and started doing the absolute bare minimum for grades and spending the rest of my time focusing on learning the ins and outs of the internet and building apps. It was these personal side things I was learning about, the projects I built on my own because I wanted to build them, that got me my internships and contracts while I was in college. It wasn't my college experience. And once I was out of college, it was my previous internships and contracts that built my career, not my college degree.

So my advice to anyone considering going to college for computer science or dropping out from their degree, take a good long look at yourself in the mirror and ask yourself these questions: 

"Do I want to do this?" 
"Can I see myself doing this for a long time?" 
"Am I learning this because I enjoy looking at an empty folder, and turning it into a codebase that does something cool?"
"Do I look stuff up on my own that has nothing to do with my coursework, because it is useful to something I want to build"

If you answered yes to these questions, it is highly likely your best career move would be to forget college.

VideoTitle: Frontend vs Backend vs Fullstack Web Development - What should you learn?
CommentText: I've been doing "full stack" development since 2012. So, I'd consider myself an expert in almost everything. Maybe not Webpack in great depth, but that's usually unnecessary for everyday work. And if it is needed, you can always find the solution in countless existing projects that use it in the way you need. Also, I don't understand why this trend of dividing a web developer into specific groups has emerged. I can only assume that some employers don't want to pay a full stack developer's salary if only (advanced) frontend skills are required. However, I've also seen some people for whom real programming is too complicated. Therefore, yes, new frontend technologies appear constantly, but companies don't have to use them. And that's also my experience: many companies have an older frontend stack, meaning no complex JavaScript, module loaders, or frameworks. If they use something like that, it's only because they have to, not because they actually need it. You'll mainly find those new school technologies used in large open-source projects/platforms, and only the departments in such companies are really specialized in one thing. The typical frontend developer, as I know them, is someone who can work with jQuery and CMS systems and has maybe heard of Vue or React but never really used them in production.

Mr. Shapiro, the Washington Post has provided a better critique than Politifact and Associate Press about 2000 Mules, covering the first movie clip addressed in this video. Like most viewers, including myself, you presumed that the film was showing the actual route of an alleged mule with accurate dropbox locations overlapped on this route. The conversation between Phillips and D'Souza in the film appears to emphasize this by stating the orange dots are drop boxes.

The Washington Post article shows however that more often than not these orange dots do not line up with dropbox locations taken from the Fulton and Gwinnett County websites in 2020. No such mistakes in drop box locations should have occurred if the data analysis was reliable and highly scrutinized by professionals, especially when True the Vote and D'Souza use it to claim the 2020 election was rigged. 

The Washington Post article notes that Phillips responded in an email that 'the movie graphics are not literal interpretations of our data' from True the Vote. This explanation for the inaccurate map was unconvincing to me for three reasons. One, would not the actual route be more compelling for advancing your claim about the 2020 election than a fake map used for dramatic cinematic effect? Two, why is there no disclaimer for the map that is shown on screen to film viewers as Phillips is presenting D'Souza the "actual" route of the alleged mule in Atlanta, Georgia? Three, if the map on screen is fake, then why does it seem to appear to also be on Phillips's laptop as he presents the route of the alleged mule to D'Souza? 

In short, if you are trying to show people that our 2020 Election was rigged, such a serious accusation should not allow deceptive visuals to substitute accurate presentations of the data for the sake of dramatic cinematic effect. Such tactics harm the credibility of the film and the presenters, rile up fanatical and delusional conspiracy theorists who won't fact check the data and present the visuals as fact to others, and can even contribute to a "boy who cried wolf" problem for legitimate investigations of election crime and insecurity during the 2020 election. 

Below I have attached the Washington Post article for reference. As stated at the beginning of this comment, it is a far better critique by the press then the intial ones you addressed in your video. Another shocking thing the Washington Post article found was that the film uses a stock photo of Moscow and presents it as if it were Gwinnett County. CommentText:
Beats >99% (1 hash map or array solution):

Intuition: Count len(s1) consecutive s1 characters in s2 without overcounting

Approach: Count len(s1) consecutive s1 characters in s2, such that
1. Start by looking for a character of s1 within s2, then try counting len(s1) consecutive s1 characters
2. Every time we encounter one of the consecutive characters, decrement map[char] by 1
3. If we manage to count len(s1) consecutive characters without overcounting, that means all of those chars are in s1, and each letter has the same count as s1
4. If there is an overcount, just keep shifting the left pointer while reversing the counts, until the overcount is fixed
5. If we encounter a non-s1 character at idx while trying to count consecutively, keep shifting the left pointer while reversing the counts, until l = idx, then set l = idx + 1

class Solution:
    def checkInclusion(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
        s1Len = len(s1)
        s2Len = len(s2)
        s1Counts = {}
        for c in s1:
            s1Counts[c] = s1Counts.get(c, 0) + 1

        l = 0
        bound = s2Len - s1Len + 1
        while l < bound:
            # if current char is a s1 char, try counting len(s1) consecutive chars
            if s2[l] in s1Counts:
                count = 0
                while count <= s1Len:
                    if count == s1Len:
                        return True
                    
                    currIdx = l + count
                    # Out of bounds or encounter non-s1 char
                    if currIdx == s2Len or s2[currIdx] not in s1Counts:
                        while l < currIdx:
                            s1Counts[s2[l]] += 1
                            l += 1
                        l = currIdx + 1
                        break

                    currChar = s2[currIdx]
                    s1Counts[currChar] -= 1
                    count += 1
                    # If there is an overcount, move left pointer until it's fixed
                    while s1Counts[currChar] == -1:
                        s1Counts[s2[l]] += 1
                        l += 1
                        count -= 1
            else:
                l += 1

        return False

VideoTitle: Why Hollywood Elites Rejected ‘Hillbilly Elegy’
CommentText:
My mom was born in 1939, the third surviving child of my Grandfather,  the oldest of 13 children in an Oklahoma farming family. Grandpa traveled some as a guitar player in a Bluegrass band until finding Christ in the mid 1930s, and settling down with his new bride near her family home in the mountains of Southern New Mexico,  in a "Town" named Picacho, really just a loose cluster of one and two room buildings that was about 15 miles from Lincoln NM, home of the "Lincoln County War that made Billy the Kid famous, and 25 miles from Capitan, known as the home of Smokey the Bear. About 70 miles away from Roswell NM, later famous for the Roswell incident.  Mom was born in one of those 2 room buildings the called a house, sadly her mother died shortly thereafter. They continued to live in Picacho for a couple of years, and I'll skip the rather crazy story about how my Grandpa managed to find a second wife, as dark side of the Waltons as it is, and it is interesting it is not relevant to my squirrel trail style of storytelling this time. What is relevant, his new wife, from ST Paul Minnesota was unhappy in a two room shack with no electricity,  no indoor plumbing, an out house, water from a creek, boiling water on a Woodstock for bathing and laundry...a way of life that the Walton family would shudder at the thought of living. So Grandpa, (Eskel  Eric Sparkman,  a very large, lean and hard built, hands that made any man feel insecure during a handshake, and a no nonsense, gruff and somewhat cold demeanor but with more integrity than about anyone I've ever known since and tough as saddle leather) moved the family to the metropolis of Roswell in a 1926 model T Ford with no reverse gear. My mom, started school a year older than her peers. She had two dresses, one a very cheap store-bought dress for church, the other a homemade, and third owner hand-me-down made from a flour sack. She had one pair of shoes, owned by at least 4 other girls before she got them. In Picacho shoes were only worn to church or if it was really cold outside (sub zero nights and mornings were common, as was snow) but obviously in the big city (30k population) shoes were more common even for toddlers. Mom wore them at school and church but went barefoot everywhere else which just made her an even more of an easy target for city kids who delighted in bullying the hillbilly girl   from Picacho.

Of course over a few years mom adapted to life on Roswell. She managed to make a friend by the time she graduated from Roswell High School but never was really accepted by her classmates, was always self conscious about her origins, and I believe felt some degree of shame and self loathing until her death at 80 yrs old in Portales NM. She died from Esophageal Cancer.  Her anxiety about going into a store and strangers somehow knowing she was "From the hills" meant she insisted my brother and I should only speak quietly, hands at our sides, eyes forwards, and never look exited about anything while in public because city people laugh at hill folk children, all exited because they only came to town once per year and would act all crazy and backwards in a store if they saw candy or toys. I don't know if her perception was reality but she believed it was and if she thought someone had figured out her true heritage she would become embarrassed and ashamed. While in her later years she got past that stuff, at least a little bit, and she learned to use a computer in her 70s, she in many ways remained a hillbilly girl from Picacho until the end. The last time I saw her, about a year before her passing (I live 1000 miles away and my situation makes travel difficult) I told her that I was very proud of her, proud that she came from tough, hard as nails yet salt of the earth folk that had a reserved sort of dignity, honor and integrity that most folks could've learned from and If anybody ever said anything mocking her roots in my presence they would learn how real the movie KinFolk actually was. My YouTube channel username or handle, whatever its called, the Oldhillbilly part is in honor of my mom, and my pride in her roots.

VideoTitle: Top 5 Most Common Graph Algorithms for Coding Interviews
CommentText: Topological sort is IMHO less obscure than Union Find or Dijsktra's. The latter are more well known by name because they are illustrative for didactics, e.g. Union Find is the first major algorithm introduced in Sedgewick's book as a case study, before returning to a more orderly review of algorithms. Topological sort is, conversely, is an extenstion to a wide variety of well known practical problems like ordering a course schedule or execution of project or (automated) job dependencies. Cracking the Code Interview even argues you should be able to derive it on the spot if you didn't know it (I disagree but shrug). Its a minor point but I think people might see it and think they should study it last, where as IMHO its more expected knowledge than Dijkstra's and also really easy to understand once you've done a few DFS problems!

CommentText:
Some name ideas for Amd:
 
Option 1: 
Ryzen AI 1 max, ryzen AI 1 plus, ryzen AI 1 super. 
For the next gen its pretty simple. We will just replace the 1 with the 2. 
So the number will be an easy indicator for the Generation...

Option 2:
Just make a Ryzen AI 1 (number as Generation indication again) a/b/c/d/e/f (A->F as "grading"). So for example it would be Ryzen AI 1A, Ryzen AI 1B, Ryzen Ai 1C..., Ryzen AI 2A,....

The advantage of a short Word and number combination is, that you can (similar to Apple's M series) just say: "AI 1 chip" or "AI 1b chip". The same goes for my first Suggestion. This way its easier to market, build a name/brand (similar to apples M series) and have a naming scheme for the future.

The reason i would prefer option 1 more, is that a grading system can have a negative effect for the human mind. It could degrade models instead of uplifting others (that is up to marketing though). "Oh i only got the AI 1f chip. But i know that there are versions up to AI 1a." Something like that...

So to sum it up: 
The brand name should be
"Ryzen AI 'Number for gen' 'specification' ". 
For example:
(option 1) "Ryzen AI 1", "Ryzen AI 1 Plus", "Ryzen AI 1 Max", "Ryzen AI 1 Pro" 
or 
(option 2) "Ryzen AI 1a", "Ryzen AI 1b", "Ryzen AI 1c", "Ryzen AI 1d", "Ryzen AI 1e", "Ryzen AI 1f".

CommentText:
1. `!` is the logical NOT operator in JavaScript. It's used to negate (invert) the value of a boolean expression. For example, `!true` evaluates to `false`, and `!false` evaluates to `true`.

2. In this context, `username` is being implicitly coerced into a boolean value. This means it's being converted to either `true` or `false` based on its "truthiness" or "falsiness" in JavaScript.

3. JavaScript treats certain values as "falsy" when converted to boolean. These values include `undefined`, `null`, `0`, `NaN`, `''` (an empty string), and `false`. If `username` has one of these values, it will be considered falsy.

4. So, `!username` will be `true` if `username` is falsy, and `false` if `username` is truthy.

5. The `if` statement checks the result of `!username`. If it's `true` (meaning `username` is falsy), the code inside the `if` block will execute.

In short, `if (!username)` checks if `username` is not provided (`undefined`) or is an empty string (`''`). If it's not provided or empty, the code inside the `if` block will execute. If `username` has any value other than `undefined` or an empty string, the `if` block will not execute.

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge 171: Wave Function Collapse
CommentText:
Not sure if I did exactly what you did or not, because I got inspired after watching a few minutes (and JavaScript programming, unless it's FP, is kinda painful) and wrote where I thought this was going in functional programming in Kotlin.

I'm at 16:00 and the way I structured it was:
1. Set of nodes to be assigned (e.g. positions in the grid) of type T
2. Possible assignments (e.g. the five road blocks) of type V
3. A set of rules:
    If, for a node t, you assign a value v, then how does this affect the choices of assignments to all the other tiles?
    So my typealiases / data structures are:
    - Assignment<T, S>
    - Possibilities<T, Set<S>>
    - Then the rules are:
       Map<Assignment<T, S>, Possibilities<T, Set<S>>

Start off with:
* possibleAssignments<T, Set<S>> where you have a T for each position / node T and where the Set<S> contains the full list of values

Every time you fix a value (either using the input seed or via picking an unfixed tile of lowest entropy), say t to s, you apply the rules for that assignment to the possibleAssignments for every other tile t'. This is just:
    possibleAssignments[t'] setintersection rules[assignment(t, s)][t']
which gives us the set of assignments we can now assign to t'

If at any point, the lowest entropy is 0, we have a problem where there is a tile that has no possible assignments and we backtrack to the point where we made an assignment choice, and make the next choice.

You can stop after you find one set of assignments that map a value to every tile, or you can find all of them.

I started with the roads, and then moved to Sudoku (where the rules are more complicated because they don't only apply to adjacent tiles of the assignment), 16x16 Sudoku, and finally, three dimensional 8x8x8 Sudoku, all of which worked well in relatively fast time.

I don't think I'll be able to move it to much higher Sudoku problems due to the combinatorial explosion, but this could definitely be used in all sorts of different types of problems where you have a set of nodes and a set of assignments and can write out the rules as above. I'm trying to apply it to some more combinatorial problems now, but music would be interesting too, as would some kind of more complicated imaging patterns. This could probably even be used in games, e.g. possibly something simplistic like tic-tac-toe or something of that variant (possibly connect four, provided you change the meaning of entropy slightly).

VideoTitle: When Someone You Love Dies,There Is No Such Thing as Moving On | Kelley Lynn | TEDxAdelphiUniversity
CommentText: I am lost. I just lost my dad. Out of nowhere. He was my go to. My person. The fixer. The one who held everything together. The one who I went to when i needed that healing love and hug. He was here this morning, when I left for work. I was just leaving work when I got a call from my mom, that my dad had fallen while walking the dog. I thought I was rushing to a scene where he had fallen and severely twisted his ankle or broken his leg. Instead, he was taken away in an ambulance and he was in such a state, that my mom was told she could not ride along in the ambulance. She was told by first responders, that she was not allowed to ride to the hospital, with the love of her life and her best friend, while she believed he was suffering. She knew. By the time I arrived, in under 5 minutes, she was a wreck. She looked at me and said "it's really bad. Very bad." Within the time it took to drive to the location, get my mom and the dog, drop the dog off at home and speed to the hospital, I already had the feeling I would never get to speak to my father, ever again. I was right. Just as my mom had said. I don't even know where to go from here. He was my rock. The fixture of our family.

VideoTitle: Minivans for life! Although @mobile_mama_reviews car looks awesome! We are gonna drive this
CommentText: When I first learned to drive, I had to operate a Chevy Suburban for a while.  I mostly disliked it from the very beginning. During a period when I was helping my dad with a house he was renovating, he had a friend who I sometimes worked with and other times I’d accompany him to get supplies. He drove a Nissan Quest. One day he asked me to drive, and I immediately noticed some differences between a minivan/normal van (more on this later). One of the biggest things I noticed was that, despite having less space because it was smaller than the SUV, I actually felt more comfortable when I sat down. Not only did I feel more at ease sitting in it, but I could also tell that it felt much better to drive. For once, I could actually sense where the wheels were, and I didn’t have to be as cautious since I could see them in my mirrors. The steering wheel was easier to turn, and I had better visibility of oncoming traffic because it didn’t sit as high as in the Suburban. Keep in mind that this was my first time driving a van, and it made a big impression on me. One thing that didn’t surprise me, since I had some prior knowledge, was the amount of stuff we could carry. Although the van wasn’t as big as the Suburban, it could actually hold the items we needed, and because of the lower height, I didn’t have to struggle as much as if we had used the SUV. Overall, the van seemed better for daily driving and work-related tasks than the SUV. The two things the van was lacking in comparison to the SUV were towing capacity and MPG. However, both of these things are… I'm not sure how to describe it... questionable?… when you consider that the guy told me he had towed things with the van without any problems in the past, and the MPG isn’t really comparable given that the Suburban was newer. While I can’t recall the van’s exact year, I know it was from the late 1980s or 1990s (again, I don’t remember the specific year). Later, I watched a video from NotJustBikes discussing SUVs (I recommend you watch their videos, they go into detail and know much more than I am explaining here), and then another video from a YouTuber that didn’t go as deep but still had some good information on the subject. In both videos, they talked about safety, and to those who believe that "well, surely the SUV is safer than a van," I’m sorry to tell you, but that isn’t actually the case. Yes, the SUV will protect you if you get into a collision with a regular-sized car. However, most cars these days (at least in America) are SUVs. If you happen to collide with someone and you’re both in SUVs, you are at a higher risk of injury, or worse, than if you were both in sedans. This is because of a phenomenon known as crash compatibility. It’s when two cars work together during a collision to minimize the risk of injury to both drivers at the expense of the vehicles taking most of the damage. However, this isn’t as effective with SUVs, because they are categorized as “trucks.” Due to strange and illogical laws here in the US, trucks aren’t held to the same safety standards as regular cars. They are also not held to the same emission standards as cars. Because of this, many of them are not safety tested (I’m not sure if that’s the correct terminology), and they don’t actually have great MPG. The “bigger is safer” argument isn’t really valid when they aren’t tested for safety in the first place. You are just being sold the illusion of safety. This is because automakers here in the US would rather produce SUVs to avoid crash testing and meeting emissions standards. I'm going to stop rambling since I've already written a lot and don't want to spend another 30 minutes writing more, so I'll get to the point. I'm starting to get political 💀 They aren’t great for off-roading. They aren’t ideal for daily use. They aren’t particularly good for work. They are expensive. In general, there are better options. A hatchback is better most of the time (I haven’t driven one, but I have ridden in one, and it was better than the Suburban we had). I'm 18, and I don't know why I just talked so much about SUVs and how they aren't great. I just saw two guys arguing about whether SUVs were good or not, and I simply wanted to share my opinion and some facts for you guys to understand it better. In summary, if you know you do a lot of off-roading, I would recommend a van, a hatchback, or a genuine truck. If you don’t go outdoors much and just travel to and from work, a sedan is always going to be better. And if you want a family vehicle, a van will always be better on gas, more comfortable, and better to drive. And if you want something better than a van, then a hatchback is the way to go. If you’re going to get a truck, make sure you work in construction or some other job that involves heavy loading, and not if you work in an office. Overall, SUVs aren’t good in any situation, and there are better options. Don’t buy them to look cool. Trust me, I'm not impressed, and I'm pretty sure the other guy isn't either. I recommend watching NotJustBikes's video on the topic. I'll leave now because I need to stop rambling.

Regarding JSON vs YAML: It's not only about performance, but also about validation and security.
If you, e.g. copy+move some lines from a JSON file to another location, most likely, the JSON will be corrupt and incorrect, and if not, it's very likely, the order didn't matter anywhere. That's good behaviour for anything that mainly computers operate, as such a copy+paste error easily happens while editing (or merging with git), but might not be reviewed by (many) humans, so might be undetected for a long time. In YAML, there is a good chance, randomly moving blocks around, the end result is a different, but still correct YAML. Indeed, that's such a common error, that for bigger projects you usually have to write an own linter for the yaml files checking e.g. if the keys are the expected ones. Regarding security: YAML specification is a bit bigger than XML, so it contains a lot of hard to implement and possible insecure options. That's why many first naive implementation of YAML parsers in programming languages were replaced over time by other parser only implementing a secure subset of YAML. (Or alternatively that's tackled by the custom linters you have to write anyway)

There are some other subtle problems with YAML, e.g. your question of why you have to put "3.8" in quotes is because otherwise it would be detected as float und depending of whether can be represented in binary internally exactly or only close to it (indeed, 3.8f == 3.7999999523162841796875). The easiest way to enforce consistency is to demand that the version is always a string and not sometimes a string (3.8.0 == "3.8.0"), sometimes a float (3.8 == 3.7999999523162841796875) and sometimes an int (4 == 4).
There are many more subtle possibilities to misinterpret the unquoted strings: Magic words like true or false are becoming booleans. A minus sign is very often interpreted as list start, several further characters like +, |, <, > also have special meanings and so on. When in doubt, always put your strings into quotes, from a practical standpoint that the system should what we want to say in the yaml, even though readability is reduced.

That's why, where high predictability is wanted, often enough different formats are used with less surprisings. E.g. HCL for Terraform, Programming languages for Pulumi, AWS CDK, ... or just toml/ini files.
Anyway, the high readability, easy understanding and universal structure of YAML dominates pretty much every modern stack, so the solution to all the above problems are custom linters and performant YAML parsers (most often with an own subset or dialect).

BTW, JSONs have disappointing also ambiguities that can even be exploited, e.g. the spec does not tell anything what should happen if a key is duplicated (which value to take). Different parsers handle that differently, and for the right combination, you can pass the validation done by the first parser to then inject some malicious (or just unintended, unwanted) behaviour to the second parser.

CommentText: Its so crazy cuz when i was a kid (im 35 now) every single person i knew had a house, car, no matter what job they had, the mail lady lived next door to us in a house, a fire fighter lived on the other side, a few of our neighbors worked in factories, a couple worked at the local grocery shop, all had nice homes... I can remember when divorce was few and far between. I used to feel like my parents generation was so far away from mine but when i look back i realize we were much closer to their ways than to how the world is now. CommentText: I began programming with Logo and Basic (not VB) during the days of monochrome monitors on a Vic-20 and Apple IIe. Later, I transitioned to Pascal and C on PC clones. I used to really enjoy developing multimedia projects using Director back in the early 90s. In combination with Photoshop and Illustrator, the three tools revolutionized presentations and interactivity. These tools gave us the ability to do everything (or as much as our zip disks could hold!). Compared to today's tools, it all seems impossibly rudimentary, but it was cutting-edge for the time. Multimedia Toolbox was also another popular app, if I remember correctly. I spent hours trying to get Director to function (without success) as a front-end for databases like SQL Server. After Director, we all shifted to Flash (which was also a Macromedia app back then), spending countless hours with ActionScript and OOP. This was all way before Adobe bought everything up. Moreover, the menu's links are always clickable, even when hidden. As you can imagine, this can lead to difficult to find bugs. CommentText:
"most languages" == C/C++/C#? Many of your "most languages" comments don't apply to Lua, Ruby, JavaScript, Perl, PHP, Io, etc.. Python's core behavior is generally consistent with other dynamically-typed languages (which also tend to be interpreted, as well).

Also, instead of saying that the type of a variable is assigned at runtime, and can change, I'd say "variables are references to values, and **values** have types, and just like a sticker you can pick up the variable and stick it on a different value later". This also explains why `i++` does not work. If you have i=7 and then wrote i++ you don't want change the value 7 to be 8; that would be terrible if integers were mutable. You want to re-assign i to be a label on a new value. (Which is not to say that i++ couldn't be syntax sugar for i = i + 1, but it does help make it clear what's happening.)

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge 167: Ulam Spiral of Prime Numbers
CommentText:
My favorite prime test for large numbers is Miller-Rabin using the first 100 primes for the base unless I need certainty for really big numbers. I know that Miller-Rabin is certain up to 3,317,044,064,679,887,385,961,981 when using the first 13 primes for the base. If you need absolute certainty, I'd use the AKS test, but that takes forever for very large numbers. In your case, because you need all numbers from 1 to N, I'd use the Sieve of Eratosthenes. If I need to test small numbers, I'd use your division test, and possibly make it run faster by testing with the first 100 primes, which, can test out to 292681 without more numbers.
I ran the Sieve of Eratosthenes, the Miller-Rabin test with prime divisions first using the first 13 primes, and the AKS test up to 100000 once and found that the first two were milliseconds to seconds while AKS took 40 hours.

Same logic applies today: Putin has to fear a real military move in the Kurile, Sahalin and he must keep there reserves instead of sending them to Ukraine.
